discovery: Optical lattice atomic clocks reaching 10^-18 accuracy and their use as probes of fundamental physics

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision measurement
motivation: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock (2001-2003), trapping thousands of neutral atoms so that the lattice light leaves the clock transition unperturbed, which removes motional and light-shift errors while keeping the stability of many atoms. Ye turned the concept into the world's most precise clocks, reaching systematic uncertainties near 10^-18 and below and using ultrastable lasers, a degenerate Fermi gas and many-body control. Together they improved timekeeping by roughly two orders of magnitude over caesium standards. These clocks are a new measurement paradigm. They resolve the gravitational redshift over millimetre height differences within a single atomic sample, enable relativistic geodesy (Katori's Tokyo Skytree measurement), constrain variations of fundamental constants and ultralight dark matter, and now drive the redefinition of the SI second. This is precision measurement at its best: conceptually clean ideas that open windows onto gravity and new physics.
